sm: The hosts note that the show often covers what is wrong in the country, but with the holidays approaching it is worth highlighting what is going right. Americans give hundreds of billions of dollars to charity each year. One major example is Convoy of Hope, a faith-based humanitarian organization that provides billions of dollars in food, disaster relief, and community support around the world. In this episode, the hosts speak with Ethan, the organization's Vice President of Public Engagement, who explains what life is like for a nonprofit in America today. The episode is hosted by John Bickley and Georgia Howe.

Ethan joins from Convoy of Hope's World Distribution Center in Springfield, Missouri, the largest of three such centers, at about 170,000 square feet. The others are in Atlanta and Sacramento, placed to reach people in need more quickly. He says the organization's driving passion is to feed the world and end generational poverty in three main ways. A children's feeding program serves more than 677,000 children every school day, tying meals to schools so kids can build a foundation. A women's empowerment program teaches job skills and provides equipment so women can start businesses. Agriculture work on 80 acres in Missouri teaches self-sufficiency, so people can grow their own food. In the United States, the group also supplies groceries to families during school breaks, and it has already carried out 79 disaster responses this year.

Asked how he measures long-term effectiveness, Ethan tells of a Nepalese village hit by the 2015 earthquake. After Convoy of Hope taught agriculture there, one farmer's yearly income rose from 1,500 rupees to 60,000. The village now runs on its own and has become a farming model for Nepal, so the group has moved on. The organization works in about 42 countries with ongoing programs and has worked in 139 when disaster responses are counted. Disasters often open doors in hostile countries, as in Haiti after the 2010 earthquake. On efficiency, he says more than 90 cents of every dollar goes where donors intend, buildings were paid for by donors so there is no debt, and volunteers keep costs down. They also give only items well within expiration dates, to show dignity to those served.

Asked about skepticism toward NGOs that work with governments, Ethan says less than 1 percent of the group's income comes from government grants. It partners mainly with local churches, which know their communities, as with a recent Florida hurricane response where 900 cars came through a church parking lot daily. Partners are built over years and vetted, so money and supplies can move quickly after disasters, including in Poland. On mission creep, he says the group knows its lane, with logistics a huge part of it, and must say no to good things in order to do great ones. Still, it remains nimble, ranking number 27 on the Forbes list. It recently opened a manufacturing and packaging facility to package food and household staples. The hosts praise the group's consistent place in the Forbes top 100, and Ethan notes its strong Charity Navigator score.
